>_ BEFORE YOU READ
What question does this article answer? Core question: How can circles that only spin at constant speeds trace an outline as irregular as a raven?
Useful background: Points in the plane written as complex numbers, and eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θe^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθ. The rest is built up step by step.
Reading route: Play with the figure first. Then follow one rotating arrow, a sum of arrows, how their sizes are found, and how many are worth keeping.
When the homepage loads, a pen at the end of a chain of spinning circles draws the raven’s outline before the ASCII portrait appears. That animation is a Fourier series: a closed curve written as a sum of rotations. The figure below uses the same coefficients as the homepage. Change the number of circles and watch the outline sharpen.
.:=++++++*%@@@%#+: .+#%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@*: .-+%@@@@@@@@@@@@- .#@@@@@@@@@@@@. -*#%@@@@@@@@@+ -#%@@@@@@@@@@@@# .+%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@. :*@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@+ .*@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@% .+@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@% .+%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@+ .+%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@# .=%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@%= =%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@#=. -%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@*=: -**%@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@= :*@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@%*=*@@% .*@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@%%@# .*@@: =@@@@@@@@@%@@@%*=: .-##: .+%+. -%@@@@@@@@**@%*-. =#*: .+#=. .*@@@@@@@%+::=: =%@#*=-#@%*+==-. -%@@@@@%*-. . ........:...:. %@@%#+-. 8 circles RMS — Energy — Ⅱ Pause Show circles Number of circles 12383296320 Spectrum: |cₙ| sorted from largest (log scale)
The dashed outline is the reference curve made from all 320 terms. The solid line uses only the largest K. RMS is the root-mean-square distance between the two curves as a share of the raven’s height. The bars below show every term’s size; highlighted bars are in use. A closed curve is a function of time # Imagine tracing the raven’s outline once at a steady pace, taking one unit of time for the whole loop. At each time ttt the pen has a position (x(t),y(t))(x(t), y(t))(x(t),y(t)). Writing that position as a single complex number turns the drawing into one function:
z(t)=x(t)+i y(t),0≤t<1.z(t) = x(t) + i\,y(t), \qquad 0 \le t < 1.z(t)=x(t)+iy(t),0≤t<1.Because the outline is closed, the pen returns to its starting point: z(t+1)=z(t)z(t+1) = z(t)z(t+1)=z(t). The curve is a periodic function, and periodic functions are what Fourier series describe.
One rotating arrow # The simplest periodic motion in the complex plane is
c e2πint.c\,e^{2\pi i n t}.ce2πint.Here ccc is a complex number and nnn is an integer. As ttt runs from 0 to 1, this point moves around a circle:
its radius is ∣c∣|c|∣c∣; its starting angle is the angle of ccc; it completes nnn full turns; positive and negative nnn rotate in opposite directions; with n=0n = 0n=0 it does not move. That term fixes the drawing’s centre. Set the figure to 1 circle: the pen moves around a single circle. It is the raven’s largest term, with n=1n = 1n=1, and sets the overall size of the loop.
Arrows placed tip to tail # One arrow can only draw a circle. To draw something more complex, connect several arrows: the second starts at the tip of the first, the third at the tip of the second, and so on.
In the complex plane, placing arrows tip to tail is simply addition: adding two complex numbers joins the arrows that represent them. So the end of the chain is the sum of all the arrows:
z(t)=c0+c1e2πit+c−1e−2πit+c2e4πit+c−2e−4πit+⋯=∑ncn e2πint.\begin{aligned} z(t) &= c_0 + c_1 e^{2\pi i t} + c_{-1} e^{-2\pi i t} \\ &\quad + c_2 e^{4\pi i t} + c_{-2} e^{-4\pi i t} + \cdots \\ &= \sum_{n} c_n\, e^{2\pi i n t}. \end{aligned}z(t)​=c0​+c1​e2πit+c−1​e−2πit+c2​e4πit+c−2​e−4πit+⋯=n∑​cn​e2πint.​Each arrow still turns at its own constant speed, but joined together, their end traces a path far more complex than any single circle. This sum is the curve’s Fourier series. Each cnc_ncn​ sets the size and starting angle of one circle.
Start with the simplest pair: add the second-largest term, n=−1n = -1n=−1, to n=1n = 1n=1. It turns as fast as the first arrow, but in the opposite direction. While the large arrow makes one turn, the small arrow on its tip makes one turn the other way, stretching the pen’s path into an ellipse:
n = 1 n = −1 their sum The large arrow (n=1n = 1n=1) turns once while the small arrow (n=−1n = -1n=−1) turns once the other way. The pen traces the same ellipse as “2 circles” in the interactive figure. Then keep adding terms in the interactive figure above:
3 circles: adding n=−2n = -2n=−2 starts to bend the loop. After that: keep adding circles and watch when the beak, wing and tail appear. Finding the size of each circle # Now reverse the question: given the raven’s outline z(t)z(t)z(t), how do we find each cnc_ncn​?
The key is a simple fact: an arrow that makes a whole number of turns averages to zero over one loop. It spends equal time pointing in every direction, and those directions cancel:
∫01e2πimt dt=0,m≠0.\int_0^1 e^{2\pi i m t}\, dt = 0, \qquad m \ne 0.∫01​e2πimtdt=0,m=0.Suppose we want c3c_3c3​. Multiplying the whole curve by e−2πi⋅3te^{-2\pi i \cdot 3t}e−2πi⋅3t makes every arrow turn three extra times in the opposite direction:
the n=3n = 3n=3 arrow’s rotation is cancelled exactly, leaving c3c_3c3​ standing still; every other arrow now makes n−3n - 3n−3 turns, still a non-zero whole number. Averaging over one loop, every arrow that still turns averages to zero, and only the motionless c3c_3c3​ remains. The same works for any nnn:
cn=∫01z(t) e−2πint dt.c_n = \int_0^1 z(t)\, e^{-2\pi i n t}\, dt.cn​=∫01​z(t)e−2πintdt.In practice a computer has samples, not a continuous curve. The homepage outline was traced from the ASCII raven itself and sampled at N=2048N = 2048N=2048 points z0,z1,…,zN−1z_0, z_1, \dots, z_{N-1}z0​,z1​,…,zN−1​ around the loop, the kkk-th point at time t=k/Nt = k/Nt=k/N. Replacing “the average over one loop” with “the average of these 2,048 points” turns the integral into a sum:
cn=1N∑k=0N−1zk e−2πink/N.c_n = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} z_k\, e^{-2\pi i n k / N}.cn​=N1​k=0∑N−1​zk​e−2πink/N.This is the discrete Fourier transform (DFT). 2,048 points give 2,048 coefficients, and the fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes them all efficiently. This was done once, when the animation was made; your browser only reads the results.
Which circles to keep # Of the 2,048 possible terms, the homepage keeps 320. The choice is simple: sort by radius ∣cn∣|c_n|∣cn​∣ and keep the largest. The figure’s spectrum shows the same ordering.
The reason comes from Parseval’s theorem. If zKz_KzK​ keeps only some of the terms, the average squared distance between the two curves equals the total squared size of the terms that were dropped:
∫01∣z(t)−zK(t)∣2 dt=∑n dropped∣cn∣2.\int_0^1 \bigl|z(t) - z_K(t)\bigr|^2\, dt = \sum_{n \text{ dropped}} |c_n|^2.∫01​​z(t)−zK​(t)​2dt=n dropped∑​∣cn​∣2.Every dropped term adds its own ∣cn∣2|c_n|^2∣cn​∣2 to the error, and the terms do not interfere with each other. So for a fixed number of circles, keeping the largest ones gives the smallest average squared error. The figure’s RMS and energy readouts are computed directly from this identity.
Compared with the 320-term curve:
Circles Energy kept RMS gap (share of height) 1 86.62% 15.4% 2 91.56% 12.3% 3 95.69% 8.8% 8 99.15% 3.9% 32 99.98% 0.58% 96 > 99.99% 0.16% Energy here means ∑∣cn∣2\sum |c_n|^2∑∣cn​∣2 over the rotating terms. The first eight circles already hold more than 99% of it. The remaining 1% is what separates a blob from a raven.
What the circles find hard # Smooth, gently curving stretches are cheap: low frequencies describe them well. Sharp corners such as the tip of the beak, the claws and the tail are expensive. A corner changes direction suddenly, and only fast-turning arrows can follow that. With few circles every corner is rounded off; more circles make the corners sharper.
That is why the spectrum has a long, slowly shrinking tail. Among the 32 largest terms, the fastest turns 25 times per loop. Among the 96 largest, it turns 68 times. Further down the list, some kept terms turn up to 1,023 times per loop, the highest frequency 2,048 samples can represent. Every term faster than 200 turns, however, has a radius under 0.004% of the raven’s height. They hardly change the picture.
From the formula to the homepage # The same mathematics shaped some engineering choices:
The homepage does not compute the series. A short script, generate_raven_path.py, adds up all 320 terms in advance and stores every point of the 2,048-sample loop as a 16-bit integer pair. The browser only decodes them. The homepage draws at most 96 circles. Circles with a radius under 0.2 pixels cannot be seen. The outline still uses all 320 terms, so skipping tiny circles only simplifies the illustration. This page computes the curve in your browser because you choose the number of circles. Recomputing 2,048 points from up to 320 terms takes no more than a few hundredths of a second. How this website is built describes the site around these pieces.
Circles on circles # Drawing with circles on circles is an old idea. Ancient astronomers described planetary motion with epicycles: a small circle whose centre moves around a larger one. A Fourier series is the same construction with as many circles as needed. Given enough of them, it can follow almost any closed path. That flexibility explains both why epicycles could match observations well and why a good fit alone does not show that a model explains the motion.
The raven on the homepage is not a planet, but the principle is the same: 320 circles, each turning at its own constant speed, are enough to draw it.
summary: A Fourier series explained through the homepage raven: rotating arrows, the discrete Fourier transform, and why keeping the largest circles works.
title: Drawing a raven with circles

The guitar neck is a grid. Each fret raises a string by one semitone, and neighbouring strings are a perfect fourth apart (five semitones), except G to B, which is a major third (four). Once you see that grid, a scale stops being a list of note names and becomes a pattern you can move.
Scales on the fretboard # Choose a root and a scale. Notes shows note names; Degrees shows each note’s role in the scale: 1 is the root, ♭3 a minor third above it, 5 a perfect fifth. Tap a position to hear it, or play the scale up and back down an octave.

Tap any position to hear it; scroll sideways for the whole neck. With a keyboard, Tab into the neck, move with the arrow keys and press Enter to play.
A few things to try:
Move the root. Change A to C and the whole pattern slides three frets up the neck. The shape stays the same; only its position changes. Find the box. A minor pentatonic between frets 5 and 8 is the shape most guitarists learn first: two notes on every string. Compare major and natural minor. Switch to Degrees and change only the scale: the 3rd, 6th and 7th drop by a semitone, everything else stays. Hear the blues note. The blues scale is minor pentatonic plus one note, the ♭5, which sits between 4 and 5. Hearing intervals # An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in semitones. On one string that is simply the number of frets between them: five frets up is a perfect fourth, seven a perfect fifth, twelve an octave.

The ear trainer needs JavaScript to play sound.
Start with the Starter set and rising intervals. Hum the two notes back before answering: if you can sing it, you have heard it. Then try falling intervals, which most people find harder, and finally both notes together. Your accuracy for each interval is kept only in this browser, so you can see which ones need work.

content:
Building a personal website no longer requires learning web development from scratch first. With a coding agent such as Codex or Claude Code, you can describe your requirements, create pages, adjust layouts, and set up publishing, then refine the result through previews.
Still, “build me a website” leaves many decisions to the tool. Where should articles live? Where will the site be hosted? How will you update it? Does your computer need to stay on?
This article uses the website you are reading as an example. It introduces the main components and their roles, so you can use its architecture as a reference, describe what you want, and work with a coding agent on the implementation.
The big picture: from articles to a website # The basic process is to turn text files and templates into pages, then let a hosting platform serve them to readers.
Articles, images, settings + Blowfish theme ↓ Hugo generates the site ↓ HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images ↓ GitHub Pages / Cloudflare ↓ Reader's browser Component Its role on this site Markdown Holds articles and page content Hugo Combines content, settings, and templates into website files Blowfish Provides the appearance and common reading interfaces Git / GitHub Stores source files and revision history GitHub Actions Automatically builds and publishes updates GitHub Pages Hosts the primary public website Cloudflare Hosts another copy as a mirror Codex / Claude Code Helps connect the components, adjust the design, and check results To begin, you can use Hugo, a theme, and one hosting platform. Publishing to two platforms is a choice made for this site; you do not need both from the start.
Static websites: prepare the pages before readers arrive # A static website has its main page content generated before publication. When someone opens an article, the server sends existing HTML, styles, and images, which the browser displays.
Think of it as a typeset ebook: after adding or editing content, you generate an updated copy and put it online.
This works well for personal profiles, research publications, portfolios, technical notes, and blogs. Their content is usually updated by the author, so there is little need to assemble each page from a database whenever someone visits.
Maintenance is relatively simple, too. This site does not require me to manage a continuously running application and database. Once published, it remains available even when my computer is off.
“Static” does not mean the page cannot move. The galaxy, terminal, and raven interactions on this site run as JavaScript in the browser. Theme switching, expandable content, and article search using a prebuilt index can also work on a static site.
Features that need server-side processing require additional planning: signing users in, storing individual users’ data, or collecting payments, for example. If your main goal is to present your work and write articles, a static website is an approachable starting point.
Hugo: turning content into pages # Hugo is a static site generator. You supply articles, images, settings, and templates; it combines them into a complete website.
Articles are mainly written in Markdown, a text format with simple formatting markers. For example, ## introduces a section heading, and **text** makes text bold. The source remains readable and is easy to work on with a coding agent.
An article might look like this:
--- title: "My first article" date: 2026-10-05 draft: true --- This is the opening paragraph. ## Why build a website? I want somewhere to collect my work and notes. ... The information between the two --- lines is called front matter. It tells Hugo the title, date, and whether the article is a draft. The body follows below.
Hugo also supports multilingual websites. This site’s English and Traditional Chinese pages are written separately and linked through the language switcher. The translations still need to be prepared and checked; Hugo organises them and generates the pages.
For everyday writing, you edit the content while templates take care of navigation, footers, and article layout. As the collection grows, this avoids repeatedly editing the same elements on individual pages.
Blowfish: start with a complete design, then make it your own # Hugo generates the website; the theme supplies its presentation. This site uses Blowfish, a Hugo theme with article layouts, navigation, and light and dark appearances.
A theme gives you a usable site early on. You can add a profile and a few articles, check the structure, and then adjust typography, colours, the homepage, and interactions.
The current homepage includes custom elements such as a research galaxy, a profile panel, and an ASCII raven. These build on the theme: I used Codex to modify HTML templates, CSS, and JavaScript to create the appearance and interactions I wanted.
For example, you could ask:
Use a dark background on the homepage. Show my name, research interests, and contact details first. On mobile, place those details before interactive decorations. Keep article pages quiet and easy to read.
Specific requirements make it easier to judge the preview. Once you can see the result, refine it one change at a time.
GitHub and GitHub Actions: save the content and automate updates # Git records file changes, and GitHub hosts Git repositories. Changes to articles and designs can have a recorded history, making it easier to compare revisions or recover an earlier version.
This site keeps source content and editing history in a private repository. The public repository contains only the generated website files. Readers can access published pages, while drafts, internal notes, and other working files do not have to be published alongside them.
GitHub Actions automates building and publishing. When I push an update to the source repository, GitHub starts a build environment, runs Hugo, and sends the generated files to the hosting platform.
An everyday update therefore becomes: edit an article, preview it locally, push the changes once satisfied, and check that publishing succeeded.
GitHub Pages: giving the website a public address # After generating the files, you need somewhere readers can access them. GitHub Pages is GitHub’s static website hosting service.
Its role differs from the repository: the repository stores files and revisions, while Pages serves website content through a URL. This site’s primary address is https://yenjia.github.io/.
You can start with the address provided by the platform. If you later want your own domain, you can add the domain and DNS configuration. The domain is the address readers enter; the hosting platform supplies the website files.
The initial setup connects Pages with the publishing workflow. A coding agent can help with those settings, but you should still open the production URL after publishing and check the homepage, articles, images, and links.
Cloudflare: hosting the same content on another platform # Cloudflare provides several website and networking services. For static sites, you may encounter Cloudflare Pages or Workers Static Assets. Both can host website files, but their setup and deployment methods differ.
This site’s Cloudflare mirror uses Workers Static Assets. The deployment tool Wrangler uploads the files generated by Hugo. This configuration serves static content without an additional backend program for application logic.
Cloudflare Pages also allows you to upload a prebuilt website. When setting up hosting, identify which service you are using and ask the agent to follow the corresponding documentation.
On this site, GitHub Pages and Cloudflare are independent entry points built and deployed from the same source content. Cloudflare acts as a mirror. It does not sit in front of GitHub Pages, and automatic failover is not configured.
After setup, how do you write the next article? # Once the website is ready, most of your time can go into content. Here, articles live in content/posts/. Add a Markdown file with a title, date, and body, and you have the source for another article.
While writing, keep draft: true so ordinary production builds skip it. Locally, preview with drafts included:
hugo server --buildDrafts This command starts a local preview and prints its URL in the terminal. If a coding agent handles the operation, you do not need to memorize the command. It does not publish the article online. Once the content is ready, change the draft flag to false and use the existing publishing workflow.
For English and Chinese versions, you can follow this site’s naming convention: my-first-post.md and my-first-post.zh-tw.md. Place images in the project’s image directories and reference them from the article. An agent can follow the existing project structure rather than inventing a new arrangement each time.
The initial setup connects the components; later articles reuse that workflow. You can focus on writing and ask the agent for changes when you need a new layout or feature.
How to describe the project to Codex or Claude Code # Once you understand the components, you can give the agent an architecture, content requirements, and completion criteria together. Here is a starting prompt:
Build a personal website with Hugo and Blowfish, including a homepage, an About page, an article list, and research publications. Manage content in Markdown, support English and Traditional Chinese, use a dark appearance, and make it comfortable to read on mobile. Set up GitHub Actions to publish automatically to GitHub Pages. Complete local previews and build checks first, summarize the changes, and wait for my confirmation before publishing. Keep source files in a private repository and publish only generated website files. Store credentials in the platform’s secrets settings.
After the first version, assign another focused task, such as: “Display homepage publications as three cards, stacked in a single column on mobile.” Once the content and appearance are stable, add Cloudflare deployment or more elaborate interactions.
Look at the result after each round: is the text readable, does the mobile page scroll sideways, does language switching work, and are images and links intact? Ask the agent to check keyboard operation for interactive elements and ensure content remains accessible when users request reduced motion.
You do not have to memorize every command, but it helps to know which layer you are changing: content, appearance, or publishing. That makes problems easier to describe and proposed changes easier to understand.
These roles connect to make this website: Markdown holds content, Hugo and the theme generate pages, GitHub records changes, Actions automates builds, and hosting platforms provide public access. Prepare the content you want people to see, choose a simple publishing route, and work with a coding agent on the first version. You can develop it into your own website over time.
summary: Understanding each component makes it easier to describe what you want to a coding agent. This article explains how this site goes from content and design to automated publishing.
title: How this website is built: Hugo, GitHub Pages, and Cloudflare

content:
>_ BEFORE YOU READ
What question does this article answer? Core question: How can existing vision and language models be adapted into a conversational model that answers questions about medical images?
Useful background: A basic understanding of encoders, embeddings, and fine-tuning is enough; prior reading of LLaVA is optional.
Reading route: Follow the data construction, the two training stages, and then the evaluation methods. Notice how GPT-4 generates training conversations without seeing the images.
This reading note covers the original 2023 paper and was published in February 2024. Descriptions of models and tools should be read in that historical context.
Deep learning has shown promising performance on a range of medical tasks. In classification, for example, physicians can combine model outputs with their own experience to inform diagnosis. Yet many common models produce just one output for an image, such as classification logits or a segmentation mask.
A medical image can contain much more information. Some findings may relate to the target task without being its main focus—for example, an organ may show inflammation rather than a malignant tumor. Others may be unrelated to the original question but still warrant follow-up. Microsoft’s LLaVA-Med: Training a large language-and-vision assistant for biomedicine in one day, published in 2023, combines language and vision to help describe the contents of medical images.
LLaVA-Med is a conversational vision-language model. Given an image, users can ask questions or request a description, much like chatting with ChatGPT. General-purpose multimodal models available at the time of this article, such as Google Bard, could also process images and text, but their answers could be unreliable because they lacked specialized medical knowledge. This paper presents an efficient training approach that adapts existing open-source models using medical data, reporting promising results after 15 hours of training on eight 40 GB A100 GPUs.
Features and contributions # The main features and contributions can be summarised as follows:
A large, diverse dataset of medical figure-caption pairs. Open-ended instruction-following data generated with GPT-4. Two-stage training: biomedical concept alignment followed by end-to-end instruction tuning. Affordable development costs and an approach that can transfer to other domains. Low-cost serving, with inference possible on consumer GPUs. Biomedical visual instruction-following data # The two training stages require different datasets. The source is PMC-15M, a collection of 15 million image-text pairs extracted from PubMed Central. Each pair contains an image and its corresponding caption.
For stage 1, the authors randomly sample 600,000 pairs to help align visual and language representations with biomedical concepts. They call this biomedical concept alignment data. Training uses single-turn instructions, as illustrated below.
Here, X_q denotes the question, X_v the image, and X_c its caption. The model describes the image using either a brief description or a detailed description.
For stage 2, the authors sample 60,000 pairs and prepare multi-turn conversations. The images cover five modalities: chest X-rays, CT, MRI, histopathology, and gross pathology. Because the source dataset does not include multi-turn image-based conversations, GPT-4 generates them from the captions.
Crucially, GPT-4 did not see the images in this process. It received captions and prompts asking it to respond as though it could see the image, generating two or three turns of questions and answers from a visual perspective. Figure 4 illustrates this procedure. The resulting dataset is called biomedical instruction-tuning data.
Training approach # Training has two stages. Biomedical concept alignment runs for one epoch, followed by three epochs of end-to-end instruction tuning, as shown in Figure 3. Additional fine-tuning can then be performed for downstream tasks.
The approach does not depend on a special architectural trick and can be applied to other vision-language architectures. In stage 1, the model predicts image captions while the image encoder and language model remain frozen. Only the projection matrix after the image encoder is updated, with the aim of aligning visual concepts with word embeddings.
In stage 2, the language model also participates in training using the GPT-4-generated multi-turn conversations. The authors report strong zero-shot performance on some visual question answering (VQA) datasets after this stage.
Experimental results # The authors evaluate the medical chatbot in two ways. First, they construct a validation set of 193 questions, including conversations and detailed image descriptions, and use GPT-4 to score the responses. Table 1 compares LLaVA-Med with LLaVA, a model trained only on stage 1, and models trained with different amounts of data. Even with 10,000 examples, LLaVA-Med outperforms LLaVA in this evaluation, and additional data further improves performance.
The second evaluation uses three medical VQA datasets:
VQA-RAD: 315 radiology images and 3,515 question-answer pairs generated by clinicians. SLAKE (Semantically-Labeled Knowledge-Enhanced dataset for medical VQA): 642 radiology images and more than 7,000 question-answer pairs created by experienced physicians. PathVQA: 4,998 pathology images and 32,799 question-answer pairs. Questions are divided into open-ended and closed-ended categories. Open-ended answers are evaluated by the proportion of ground-truth tokens appearing in the generated answer; closed-ended answers are evaluated using accuracy. Table 3 shows promising results for LLaVA-Med in both categories.
Together with the paper’s ablation studies, these experiments suggest two main points:
Longer stage 1 training improves zero-shot transfer, but stage 1 alone is insufficient. Instruction-following data is crucial for stage 2. An additional case study # Although the training conversations use only English, the model demonstrates an ability to answer Chinese questions in the example shown in Table 6. The authors speculate that LLaMA may already have acquired some multilingual knowledge, making this transfer possible. Other existing models may not transfer to a different language as successfully in a zero-shot setting.
Conclusion # LLaVA-Med is a large vision-language model focused on biomedicine. GPT-4 is used to create medical visual instruction-following data. After further fine-tuning, LLaVA-Med surpasses other models on some evaluation metrics. It still exhibits familiar limitations of large language models, including hallucinations and limited deep reasoning. ↳ TAKEAWAYS
Three ideas and a follow-up question Data construction is part of the method: Figure-caption pairs and GPT-4-generated conversations serve different training stages. The stages have different purposes: First align visual and language representations, then learn to follow biomedical instructions. Evaluation methods shape the interpretation: GPT-4 scores, answer-token coverage, and closed-ended accuracy measure different aspects of performance. A follow-up question: Which information in an image can caption-generated conversations capture, and which information might they miss?
Scope of the evidence: Read the reported evaluations and Chinese-language example alongside the model’s hallucinations and reasoning limitations.
For further reading, start with the original paper and official code linked below.
References # Li, Chunyuan, Cliff Wong, Sheng Zhang, Naoto Usuyama, Haotian Liu, Jianwei Yang, Tristan Naumann, Hoifung Poon, and Jianfeng Gao. “LLaVA-Med: Training a large language-and-vision assistant for biomedicine in one day.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2306.00890 (2023). Microsoft LLaVA-Med repository
summary: The data, training approach, and experiments behind a conversational medical vision-language model.
title: LLaVA-Med: a vision-language model for medicine
